cards.title: COGS Drives Unit Economics and Valuation
cards.summary: Why COGS accuracy matters for ecommerce operators: it sets the cash left per unit for marketing and R&D and drives gross margin used in valuations.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product can fund its own acquisition and reinvestment, or preparing gross margin figures for investors or lenders.
steps: Take the sale price of a unit. Subtract only the true cost of delivering that unit (materials, direct labor, factory overhead, freight-in, packaging, or for digital: servers, delivery APIs, support and implementation wages depending on model).

The remaining gross profit per unit is the pool available for marketing, R&D and overhead. If gross profit per unit cannot cover customer acquisition cost plus contribution to overhead, the unit is not economically viable at that price.
Recognise that external valuers look at revenue growth and gross margin together; a misclassified cost that understates COGS inflates gross margin and distorts the valuation multiple.
Use the corrected gross margin to decide whether to make more of the same product, reprice, or discontinue and build a new product.
Keep a simple per-SKU gross profit calculation so repricing and promotion decisions are grounded in the same numbers shown to investors.
caveats: Gross margin is not the only valuation input; growth, retention and market matter too.
The source frames this for finance leaders and founders; the application to SKU-level decisions is an adaptation of that principle.

cards.title: Separate inbound inventory freight from customer delivery costs
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.
steps: Identify what the charge purchases: inventory, customer delivery, support, referral or another service.
Use the applicable accounting policy for statutory classification rather than a universal label from another business model.
Track the charge separately per order or channel where possible.
Reconcile gross profit to contribution after variable fulfillment, commissions and support costs before setting CAC limits.
caveats: Service and software examples in the source do not establish universal COGS rules for a physical-product store.

cards.title: CPG vs SaaS Cost Structures and Margin Benchmarks
cards.summary: CPG/manufacturing carries high tangible COGS and 20-40% gross margins; SaaS carries lower labor/server COGS and 70-90% gross margins.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product model to build or expand, or sanity-checking whether your store's gross margin is in a normal range for its category.
steps: For a tangible/CPG product, build COGS from raw materials, direct manufacturing labor, factory overhead (rent, equipment depreciation, maintenance, utilities), freight-in and packaging.
For a software/digital product, build COGS from server or hosting cost, third-party delivery APIs and tools, customer support wages and implementation/onboarding wages.
Compare your gross margin against the source's rule of thumb: roughly 20-40% for CPG/manufacturing and 70-90% for SaaS. The source cites a baby-food manufacturer at about 30% as typical.

When deciding where to build, weigh margin against distribution opportunity: the source notes a CPG product may take a small slice of a very large pie, while SaaS offers higher margin but depends on your skills and idea.
Do not treat the benchmarks as targets; use them to flag whether a cost has been misclassified or a price is structurally too low.
caveats: The 20-40% and 70-90% bands are the source's rule-of-thumb heuristics, not calculated thresholds for any specific store.
A CPG product with strong distribution can win on absolute profit despite low margin.

cards.title: Balance Sheet to P&L Timing for Inventory Versus Services
cards.summary: CPG costs sit on the balance sheet as inventory until sale, while many SaaS costs like wages hit the P&L immediately.
cards.use_when: Forecasting cash and monthly profitability, or explaining to a founder-investor why a stock build-up hurts cash before it hits COGS.
steps: For physical products, capitalise inventory (including freight-in) as an asset on the balance sheet when produced or purchased, then move it to COGS on the P&L only when the item sells.
Understand that building stock consumes cash now and reduces reported profit later — useful when planning seasonal buys or bulk purchasing for cost savings.

For a SaaS/digital product, most COGS (support wages, implementation wages) hits the P&L immediately; only capitalised fixed assets such as owned servers or computers flow from the balance sheet into COGS via depreciation over time.
If you rent server capacity (AWS/Azure), the monthly fee goes straight to COGS rather than being depreciated.
Use this distinction when forecasting: a stock-heavy quarter depresses cash before it depresses profit, while a services-heavy quarter depresses profit immediately.
caveats: The source notes most modern small companies rent rather than own servers; ownership changes the accounting treatment.
Inventory costing methods (e.g. FIFO/weighted average) are not covered here.

cards.title: Tie Server and Hosting Costs to Business Usage
cards.summary: Cloud costs (AWS/Azure) left unchecked rise quickly; reconcile them to customer or usage growth with engineering.
cards.use_when: Running a hosted or usage-based digital store, app or subscription platform where cloud spend is a major COGS line.
steps: Treat monthly AWS/Azure fees as COGS for a rented-server model (owned hardware instead flows in as depreciation).
Track cloud cost against usage or number of accounts so that adding a customer does not double your cost unnecessarily.
Build a per-customer or per-usage view of infrastructure cost so you can see whether economics improve or degrade as you scale.
Hold periodic meetings between finance and engineering to review how cost should move as the business grows — the source flags this as the practical control.
When onboarding a new enterprise account, tie the incremental infrastructure cost to that account so pricing reflects real delivery cost.
caveats: The source describes the meeting cadence as a practice to adopt, not a proven benchmark.
Cloud pricing and dashboards change; verify the current AWS/Azure cost tools before building reports.

cards.title: Waste Control: Expiry Rotation, Fire Sales and Inventory Controls
cards.summary: Reduce COGS leakage by moving near-expiry stock first, using fire sales to clear aged goods, logging stock in/out, and counting periodically.
cards.use_when: Managing perishable or seasonal inventory and shrink in an ecommerce warehouse or 3PL.
steps: Track expiration and obsolescence dates per SKU and ship stock with the nearest expiration first, before touching stock with a longer window.
When stock is very close to expiry, run a fire sale to move it quickly at much lower margin rather than losing it entirely.
Log inventory when it enters and when it leaves the warehouse, and run periodic physical counts — the source identifies missing outbound logging as the control gap that enables theft.
Investigate recurring count variances as a signal of shrink or process error, and feed the cost back into your COGS assumptions.
Use the same rotation logic for seasonal goods: move the oldest season first and discount aggressively before the next season lands.
caveats: Fire sales protect cash but depress margin; the source presents them as a last-resort recovery, not routine strategy.
Physical counting frequency depends on volume and risk.

cards.title: Correct COGS Gives a Trustworthy Gross Margin Signal
cards.summary: Accurate elements and timing of COGS produce the gross margin that informs unit economics and business decisions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly accounts before making product-line, pricing or discontinue decisions.
steps: Audit each COGS line for correct inclusion: goods-related costs in, selling and promotion costs out.
Audit timing: match cost to the period the sale occurs, not when the invoice arrived, for physical goods.
After corrections, recalculate gross margin and check whether it still supports the price, the acquisition cost and the overhead contribution.
Use the corrected margin to answer the operational question the source highlights: can you make more of this product, or should you discontinue and build something new?
Repeat the audit when the model changes — for example when you move from self-fulfilment to a 3PL, or from owned to rented infrastructure.
caveats: The source does not prescribe an audit cadence; monthly or quarterly review is a reasonable adaptation.
Correct accounting alone will not fix a product whose unit economics do not work.
